title: DNS in Depth
subtitle: Watch a cold DNS lookup walk from resolver to root, TLD and authoritative server, then see how TTLs, GeoDNS and failover bend the answer.
learn: The difference between a recursive resolver and an authoritative server
How root, TLD and authoritative servers cooperate to answer one question
What A, AAAA, CNAME, MX and TXT records are for
How TTL and caching trade speed against how fast changes spread
How GeoDNS and DNS-based failover steer users, and where they lag

steps.title: Names are not addresses
steps.body: Your browser wants shop.example, but networks route packets to IP addresses. Something must translate the name into a number, and no single computer holds every name on the internet. DNS solves this with a hierarchy of servers that each know a small slice, plus layers of caching so most lookups never travel far.
steps.idea: DNS is a distributed, cached, hierarchical phone book, not one big database.
steps.caption: The browser has a name and needs an IP address.

steps.title: Ask the recursive resolver
steps.body: The OS hands the question to a recursive resolver, usually run by your ISP or a public provider. Its job is to do the whole chase for you and return one final answer. It keeps a cache, so if anyone nearby asked recently, it answers instantly. Here the cache is cold, so it has to start from the top.
steps.idea: A recursive resolver does the legwork on behalf of clients and remembers the results.
steps.caption: Browser asks the resolver; cache miss.

steps.title: Root: who runs .com?
steps.body: The resolver already knows the addresses of the 13 root server identities (hundreds of anycast machines behind them). It asks one. The root does not know shop.example, but it knows who is responsible for each top-level domain, so it replies with a referral: here are the servers for .com.
steps.idea: The root only points to the right TLD servers; it never stores individual sites.
steps.caption: Root refers the resolver to the .com servers.

steps.title: TLD: who runs shop.example?
steps.body: The resolver repeats the question to a .com TLD server. The TLD servers hold one thing for every registered domain: its NS records, naming the servers the owner chose. They reply with another referral to the domain's own name servers. Still no IP address yet, just a closer signpost.
steps.idea: The TLD tier maps each registered domain to its authoritative name servers.
steps.caption: TLD refers the resolver to shop.example's servers.

steps.title: Authoritative: the real answer
steps.body: An authoritative server holds the actual records for the zone, set by the domain owner. It answers with the A record 203.0.113.7 and a TTL of 300 seconds. The resolver caches it, returns it to the browser, and the whole cold lookup took about four network exchanges, roughly 70 ms in this example.
steps.idea: Only the authoritative server is the source of truth; everything else is a cached copy.
steps.caption: Authoritative server answers; resolver caches and replies.

steps.title: Record types
steps.body: The zone holds more than one kind of record. A maps a name to an IPv4 address and AAAA to IPv6. CNAME says one name is an alias for another, so www can follow shop.example. MX names the mail servers. TXT holds free text, used for domain verification and email policy such as SPF. A CNAME cannot sit at the zone apex.
steps.idea: Pick the record type by purpose: address (A, AAAA), alias (CNAME), mail (MX), metadata (TXT).
steps.caption: Resolver asks for www and follows a CNAME to an A record.

steps.title: TTL and caching
steps.body: Two seconds later another user behind the same resolver asks for shop.example. The resolver answers from cache in about 2 ms, no root, TLD or authoritative traffic needed. Each cached answer carries a TTL that counts down; at zero it is discarded and re-fetched. Browsers and operating systems cache too, so the real lookup count is far lower.
steps.idea: A longer TTL means faster lookups and less load, but slower propagation of any change you make.
steps.caption: Warm cache: one hop, answer in about 2 ms.

steps.title: GeoDNS: different answers by place
steps.body: The owner runs one site in the US and one in Europe. A GeoDNS authoritative server looks at who is asking, usually the resolver's IP or a client-subnet hint, and returns the nearest origin. A resolver in Frankfurt gets the EU address, so the user's later connections travel a few ms instead of 90 ms. It is a rough guess: a user on a distant public resolver can be steered wrongly.
steps.idea: GeoDNS picks the answer by the asker's location, which is only as accurate as the resolver tells it.
steps.caption: Authoritative returns the EU address; browser connects there.

steps.title: DNS-based failover
steps.body: Now the EU origin dies. The authoritative server health-checks both origins, notices, and stops returning the EU address. But resolvers and browsers still hold the old answer until its TTL expires. With a 60 s TTL, some users keep hitting a dead server for up to a minute or more, since some clients ignore TTLs. That is why failover-critical records use short TTLs.
steps.idea: DNS failover works, but it is only as fast as the TTL, so short TTLs buy faster recovery at the cost of more lookups.
steps.caption: Health check fails; clients with cached answers still hit the dead origin.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.body: A recursive resolver chases the answer through root, TLD and authoritative servers, then caches it. Records express different facts: addresses, aliases, mail, metadata. TTL is the dial between speed and agility. GeoDNS and failover both build on this, and both are limited by cached answers you cannot recall.
steps.idea: DNS is a cached hierarchy; every clever trick on top inherits the TTL delay.
steps.caption: The full lookup path and the origins it steers to.

quiz.q: A resolver has no cached data for shop.example. What is the order of servers it contacts?
options: Root, then authoritative, skipping the TLD
quiz.why: The root points to the .com TLD servers, which point to the domain's authoritative servers, which hold the actual records.

quiz.q: You must move your site to a new IP tomorrow at noon. Your A record has a 24-hour TTL. What should you do beforehand?
options: Raise the TTL so resolvers cache the new value longer
Lower the TTL to a few minutes well in advance, then change the IP
Switch the record to a TXT record
quiz.why: Caches keep the old answer until the TTL expires, so the TTL must be lowered at least one old-TTL period before the change.

quiz.q: You want example.com (the zone apex) to alias to a provider hostname, and also receive mail. Which is the real problem?
options: MX records cannot point to hostnames
CNAME records only work for IPv6
A CNAME cannot coexist with other records such as MX and NS at the apex
quiz.why: A CNAME means the name is entirely an alias, so no other record types may exist at that name; apex names need NS and SOA records.

quiz.q: Your EU origin fails and DNS failover removes it, yet some users still see errors for a minute. Most likely cause?
options: Clients and resolvers are using cached answers until the TTL expires
The authoritative server has not noticed
quiz.why: DNS changes only reach users as cached copies expire, so the TTL sets a floor on failover time for those clients.

cheatsheet.def: Server that answers clients by chasing the lookup through root, TLD and authoritative servers, and caches results.
Holds the real records for a zone. Its answers are the source of truth; all other copies are caches.
Root refers to TLD servers (.com, .org); TLD servers refer to each domain's name servers via NS records.
Map a name to an IPv4 / IPv6 address. A name can have several, which gives crude load spreading.
Makes a name an alias of another name. Cannot share a name with other records, so not allowed at the zone apex.
MX lists mail servers with priorities. TXT holds text for SPF, DKIM, DMARC and domain-ownership checks.
Seconds a cached answer may be reused. Typical values: 60 s for failover records, 300 to 3600 s for stable ones.
Authoritative server varies answers by asker location or origin health. Limited by resolver accuracy and TTL lag.
